meta.title: Operation of Conductivity Meter in Pharmaceutical Analysis Laboratory

sections.purpose: To measure the electrical conductivity of pharmaceutical water samples (purified water, water for injection), buffers, and salt solutions to verify ionic content and water quality as per pharmacopeial limits.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmaceutical Analysis laboratory for quality control of purified water (IP limit: ≤ 4.3 µS/cm at 20°C), water for injection (IP limit: ≤ 1.3 µS/cm), and preparation of buffers and salt solutions.
procedure: Switch on the conductivity meter and allow 10–15 minutes warm-up.
Rinse the conductivity cell with 3–4 portions of the sample to be measured — discard rinse portions.
Immerse the conductivity cell in the sample, ensuring the electrodes and reference junction are fully submerged.
Allow the reading to stabilize (typically 30–60 seconds) before recording.
Note the temperature of the sample simultaneously — record both conductivity (µS/cm) and temperature (°C).
Apply temperature compensation: most meters have automatic temperature compensation (ATC); if manual, use the temperature correction formula.
Read and record the conductivity value on the display.
Rinse the cell with 2–3 portions of distilled water after each sample.
For routine water quality testing: test purified water at the point of use from the water purification system; compare against IP/BP limits.
Calibrate the conductivity meter using a certified standard solution (e.g., 0.01 M KCl = 1413 µS/cm at 25°C).
Record all readings, calibration results, and sample details in the water quality monitoring logbook.
Rinse the cell with distilled water and store with the cell immersed in distilled water if measurements are to resume within 24 hours; otherwise dry and store in a protective case.
precautions: Always calibrate with a certified standard conductivity solution before use — uncalibrated readings are unreliable.
Temperature has a major effect on conductivity — always record temperature simultaneously and apply correction.
Do not allow the conductivity cell to dry out — dry electrodes take longer to equilibrate.
Rinse the cell thoroughly between samples to prevent carry-over.
For purified water: use freshly collected samples — standing in open air increases conductivity due to CO₂ dissolution.
Inspect the conductivity cell for fouling or damaged electrodes — contaminated or damaged cells give inaccurate readings.
Record all out-of-specification water conductivity results and initiate investigation immediately.
